title: Companions in dharma
hookLine: a father puts his daughter's hand in a young man's hand and says one sentence
carry: companion in dharma: walking the path together

lines: A FATHER, A HAND, A HAND.
JANAKA BRINGS SITA TO THE ALTAR.
cards: If you've been to a Hindu wedding, you may know the moment, though customs vary from family to family. The fire is lit in the middle of the canopy. The priest is chanting.
The bride's father stands, takes his daughter's hand, and places it in the groom's hand. Rooms full of noisy relatives go quiet for it. That moment has an echo in the Ramayana.
Janaka, the king who found his daughter in a furrow, brings Sita to the altar, decked in jewels, and stands her across from Rama, by the fire.

teach.b: Janaka speaks to Rama: iyam sita mama suta sahadharmachari tava. This is Sita, my daughter, your companion in dharma. Accept her.
Take her hand in yours. She will be devoted to you, and follow you always, like your shadow. He pours sacred water, and the gods say well done.
Sahadharmachari is the key word. Saha, together. Dharma, the right way, duty, the path.
Chari, one who walks. One who walks the path of dharma together with you. Not a possession, not a prize, though she was won by strength: a companion on the way.
That's the Hindu teaching of marriage in one word. Janaka gives Urmila to Lakshmana, and his brother's daughters to Bharata and Shatrughna, with similar words.
Then the four couples circle the fire three times, keeping it on their right.
In a Hindu wedding the fire, Agni, is the witness; the vows are made in front of it. Flowers fall from the sky, heavenly drums sound, and the apsaras dance.
The next morning Vishvamitra says goodbye and leaves for the northern mountains.
Now the week, from the top. Ahalya's penance, and the way back.

teach.h: IYAṂ SĪTĀ MAMA SUTĀ SAHADHARMACARĪ TAVA.
teach.b: Two princes at her feet. Sita, daughter of the earth. The kings' wounded ego, and a bow lifted as if in play.
Two family lines named aloud. And today, four couples circling one fire, each pair walking dharma side by side.

how: In Hindu weddings, the kanyadana, the father's giving of the bride's hand, and the circling of the sacred fire are central rites; some families recall Janaka's words to Rama when they explain them.

o: a priest who leads the circling of the fire
one who walks the path of dharma with you
a servant who follows the bride to her new home

games.q: inside the ceremony — tap the pairs.
p: circled three times, on the right

s: he calls her sahadharmachari, his companion in dharma.
the four couples circle the fire together
keeping it on their right, three times.
Vishvamitra stays on in Mithila after the weddings
he takes his leave the next morning and goes to the northern mountains.

games.q: you're Janaka at the altar, giving your daughter's hand. what do you call her, in the text?
games.why: sahadharmachari tava: your companion in dharma, one who walks the path with you.

practice: Bring to mind one person who walks some part of your path with you, a partner, a friend, a sibling, a colleague, and picture them beside you, not ahead or behind.
On each breath in, feel their company; on each breath out, offer them yours, and if you pray, hold them in prayer.

wordCard.voice: Sahadharmachari, one who walks the path of dharma together with you. Janaka gives Sita to Rama as his companion in dharma, and four couples circle the fire together in Mithila.

orig.note: Sanskrit sahadharmacarī: she who walks the path of dharma together with you. saha (together) + dharma + carī (one who walks).

carryVoice: Your line: companion in dharma, walking the path together. Not a possession, not a prize. And that's the week.
